title.value: Single Phase and Multiphase Fluid Flow in Horizontal Wells

name.value: Stanford University, Department of Petroleum Engineering

note.value: Existence of wall inflow or outflow is the major difference between regular pipe flow and fluid flow along a wellbore. It is the wall inflow or outflow that has a significant effect on wall friction, acceleration, and flow pattern transition. Wall inflow and outflow affect wall friction shear. The influence of wall inflow or outflow depends on the flow regime present in the wellbore. Wall inflow (production well) increases the wall friction for laminar flow though it decreases the friction for turbulent flow. The opposite is true for wall outflow (injection well).New wall friction factor correlations for pipe flow with influx have been developed based on published research work and the Stanford horizontal wellbore experimental data. They can be applied to determine wall friction shear and thus frictional pressure drop for either wall inflow or wall outflow and for either laminar axial flow or turbulent axial flow.A new single phase wellbore flow model, which incorporates not only frictional, accelerational and gravitational pressure drops, but also the influence of wall inflow or outflow, is presented. The model can easily be extended to account for fluid compressibility in order to handle gas flow in wells.Many factors play a role in gas-liquid flow along a wellbore, among them are axial gas and liquid flow rates, gas and liquid inflow or outflow rates, inflow or outflow format, pipe inclination, uid properties, pipe geometry, and wellbore completions. The influences of different parameters on the wellbore flow behavior are interrelated and depend upon specific flow conditions. For gas-liquid flow in a wellbore, both homogeneous and mechanistic models are proposed. Flow models for individual flow patterns, including stratified flow, dispersed bubble flow, annular-mist flow, and intermittent flow, are developed. New criteria for transition among different flow patterns occurring in a wellbore are proposed.Transient flow models for separated gas-liquid flow and for dispersed gas-liquid flow along a wellbore are also developed. These models are applied to validate the multiple solutions existing in separated gas-liquid wellbore flow. The transient flow equations are solved numerically by using a SCM (split coefficient matrix) finite difference approach. A computer package for the numerical solution of the transient flow equations is developed. Sample numerical simulations based on the transient flow model are presented.Multiple solutions of the momentum balance equations can be troublesome in the modeling of gas-liquid flow along a pipe or a wellbore. Occurrence of multiple solution in separated gas-liquid wellbore flow depends on fluid properties, pipe geometry, flow rates, empirical correlations for the interfacial friction factor, and wall inflow or outflow rates. Regions of multiple solutions are displayed. The impact of wall inflow or outflow on the occurrence of multiple solutions and on the regions of multiple solutions is investigated. Different features of multiple solutions are observed for gas-liquid wellbore flow. Physical considerations and numerical simulation of the transient process for separated gas-liquid flow are employed to determine the physically realistic solution wherever multiple solutions exist.Predictions by the new wellbore flow models are compared with experimental data. It is found that the new wellbore flow models can provide excellent predictions of wellbore pressure drop. The mechanistic model also makes reasonable flow pattern predictions. Differences between model predictions and measurements of the wellbore pressure drop are less than 3% for all single phase flow experiments, and less than 15% for the majority of two-phase flow experiments. This is a substantial improvement over existing two-phase mechanistic models or empirical correlations.Pressure drop along a wellbore may be a crucial parameter affecting the performance of a horizontal well and should be considered simultaneously with reservoir inflow via a coupling model. A simplified transient coupling model is proposed for different parallelepiped reservoir drainage volumes containing any number of wells with any number of laterals of arbitrary configurations. Sensitivity studies using the new coupling model are conducted for different single lateral and multilateral horizontal well systems. The coupling model can be used to determine well productivity index, well indices for simulation, wellbore potential and pressure profile, and the wall inflow or outflow rate distribution for any time in the well's production/injection history.The new wellbore models, including the single phase flow model, the homogeneous gas-liquid flow model, and the mechanistic model, are readily applicable to different wellbore perforation patterns and well completions, and can be incorporated in reservoir simulators or analytical reservoir inflow models as was done in the simplified coupling model.
Ouyang, Liang-Biao. (1998). Single Phase and Multiphase Fluid Flow in Horizontal Wells. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: https://purl.stanford.edu/dc252mj5463
